Let \(N\) be the required number. Then

\[
\boxed{
N=
\frac{r(r-1)^2}{8}\,
\frac{\ell^{\,r-3}-1}{\ell-1}\,
\ell^{\,r-4}\bigl(r(r+1)+2\bigr)
}
\]

with \(\ell=2r+1\).

Here is the derivation.

Since \(2\) generates \(\mathbb F_\ell^\times\), each of the primes
\[
q,\quad q+2Q,\quad q+4Q
\]
is inert in \(\mathbb Q(\zeta)\), because all are congruent to \(q\pmod \ell\), and \(2q\equiv1\pmod \ell\) makes \(q\) a primitive residue class mod \(\ell\). Thus if an algebraic integer in \(\mathbb Z[\zeta]\) has absolute value one of these primes, it must be that prime times a root of unity. Also
\[
\widehat f(y)\equiv \sum_x f(x)=2q^2\equiv q\pmod{1-\zeta},
\]
so the sign is positive. Hence each nonzero Fourier coefficient has the form
\[
\widehat f(y)=p_y\zeta^{a_y}.
\]

Fourier inversion then shows that the \(q\)-part of the spectrum is integral only if all phases come from one point \(v\in G\), i.e.
\[
a_y=v\cdot y.
\]
Indeed, if the chosen affine hyperplanes for all projective dual lines contain \(m(x)\) through \(x\), integrality forces
\[
\ell^{r-1}\mid m(x)-\frac{\ell^{r-1}-1}{\ell-1},
\]
so \(m(x)\) takes only the two possible values corresponding to all hyperplanes being concurrent at one point \(v\).

The extra \(2Q\) and \(4Q\) spectral increments then give a unique function \(f\) for every admissible triple \((s,U,W)\). Its first moment is
\[
\sum_x f(x)x=qv.
\]
Since \(q\equiv 2^{-1}\pmod \ell\), the condition \(\sum_x f(x)x=Ps\) forces
\[
v=2Ps.
\]
So \(f\) is uniquely determined once \(s,U,W\) are chosen.

It remains to count \(s,U,W\).

The span condition gives constants \(a,b\) with
\[
1=a s_j+b(s_{j+1}+s_{j-1}).
\]
The nonconstant cyclic solutions are exactly
\[
s_j=1+A\omega^j+B\omega^{-j},
\]
where \(\omega\) is a nontrivial \(r\)th root of unity in \(\mathbb F_\ell\). The product constraints become
\[
A^r+B^r=2,\qquad \rho^r+\sigma^r=-2,
\]
where \(\rho,\sigma\) are the roots of \(X^2+X+AB\). Since \(x^r=\pm1\) in \(\mathbb F_\ell^\times\), this forces \(A^r=B^r=1\), and \(AB=C\) where \(X^2+X+C\) has two nonsquare roots. A quadratic-character count gives exactly \((r-1)/4\) possible \(C\). For each \(C\), there are \(r\) choices of \((A,B)\), and \(r-1\) choices of \(\omega\), with the duplication
\[
(A,B,\omega)\sim(B,A,\omega^{-1}).
\]
Thus
\[
\#s=\frac{r(r-1)^2}{8}.
\]

For such an \(s\), the vectors
\[
P^ts,\quad P^t(Ps-s),\quad P^t(2\mathbf1-s)
\]
span the fixed 3-dimensional space
\[
M=\langle \mathbf1,\omega^j,\omega^{-j}\rangle.
\]
Thus \(U\) must be a hyperplane containing \(M\), giving
\[
\#U=\frac{\ell^{r-3}-1}{\ell-1}.
\]

For fixed \(U\), \(W\) is a hyperplane of \(U\) avoiding the listed \(3r\) projective points in \(M\). Counting linear forms on \(M\) that do not vanish on those points gives
\[
r(r+1)+2
\]
allowable projective restrictions, and each restriction has \(\ell^{r-4}\) extensions to \(U\). Hence
\[
\#W=\ell^{r-4}\bigl(r(r+1)+2\bigr).
\]

Multiplying the independent choices gives

\[
\boxed{
\frac{r(r-1)^2}{8}\,
\frac{\ell^{\,r-3}-1}{\ell-1}\,
\ell^{\,r-4}\bigl(r(r+1)+2\bigr)
}.
\]
